extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (biotech/chem/pharma art unit TC1600) and patent prosecution staff
extracted.subtask_description: A systematic, examiner-focused method for analyzing claim language under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre-AIA second paragraph) using the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) and for writing clear, complete indefiniteness rejections in Office actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze claim language using the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI)
rubrics_metrics.description: During examination, a claim must be given its broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification as it would be interpreted by one of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with the plain meaning of claim terms unless inconsistent with the specification. Because the applicant can amend claims during prosecution, apply BRI to reduce the chance the claim issues broader than justified. Sources of plain meaning include the words of the claims, the specification, drawings, and prior art. (See MPEP 2173.01(I); 2111.01(I) Plain Meaning.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine if the metes and bounds of the claims are clear (threshold of clarity and precision)
rubrics_metrics.description: After applying BRI, if the metes and bounds of the claimed invention are not clear, the claim is indefinite and should be rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner should apply the threshold requirement of clarity and precision: if a person of ordinary skill could not interpret the metes and bounds so as to understand how to avoid infringement, a 35 U.S.C. 112(b) rejection is appropriate. (See MPEP 2173.02(II).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a sufficient and clear explanation in the Office action (avoid conclusory rejections)
rubrics_metrics.description: Only by providing a complete explanation in the Office action as to the basis for determining why a particular term or phrase is indefinite will the examiner enhance the clarity of the prosecution history record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A complete rejection should include: (1) The analysis of the claim element in view of MPEP/Rule; (2) The conclusion of that analysis; and (3) If appropriate, a statement as to how to obviate the rejection. The examiner should avoid a conclusionary rejection which merely states the claim is indefinite without supporting analysis or guidance to applicant. Provide enough information to permit applicant to make a meaningful response. (Slides: 'The examiner should avoid a conclusionary rejection'; 'A complete rejection should include: ...')

rubrics_metrics.name: Antecedent basis — lack of antecedent basis can render a claim indefinite (MPEP 2173.05(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is indefinite when it contains words or phrases whose meaning is unclear, e.g., referring to 'said X' where no earlier recitation of X appears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether a dependent claim term (e.g., 'said protein nanopores', 'said zinc anode') has clear antecedent basis in the dependency chain or specification. Under BRI, determine whether the ordinary meaning and the specification provide the necessary antecedent support. Note: failure to provide explicit antecedent basis does not always render a claim indefinite if the scope would be reasonably ascertainable by those skilled in the art (Ex parte Porter). Cite MPEP 2173.05(e) and analyze factually (examples in slides include protein nanopores lacking antecedent support and 'said zinc anode' which did have implied antecedent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent claims relying on cancelled base claims are incomplete (MPEP §608.01(n))
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim which is directly or indirectly dependent on a canceled base claim should be rejected as incomplete; if the base claim is rejected the dependent claim should be objected to rather than rejected if otherwise allowable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a dependent claim depends on a canceled claim (e.g., 'Claim 61. The composition of claim 32...'), treat it as incomplete and, for purposes of 112(b), also analyze antecedent basis. The appropriate action is rejection as incomplete and/or rejection under 112(b) if lack of antecedent basis renders it indefinite. Suggest amendments (e.g., amend to refer to a claim that recites the subject matter or delete the claim) to obviate the rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth vs. indefiniteness — breadth alone does not make a claim indefinite (MPEP 2173.04)
rubrics_metrics.description: A broad claim is not indefinite merely because it encompasses a wide scope, provided the scope is clearly defined; indefiniteness arises when claim boundaries are unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between a claim that is broad but clearly delimited (e.g., a genus that clearly defines which species are included) and a claim whose boundaries are ambiguous. Use BRI and the specification to determine whether the breadth leaves more than one reasonable interpretation of what is covered. Example in slides: a method 'providing an insect inhibitory amount' was broad but definite because BRI included generic application to an insect and the specification showed ways of providing the protein.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unclaimed essential matter — claims must interrelate essential elements (MPEP 2172.01)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim fails to interrelate essential elements of the invention as defined by the specification, it may be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) as indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether the claim omits an essential element required to give life, meaning, and vitality to the claimed invention. If so, the claim may be indefinite even if other language is clear. Apply this when a preamble/purpose suggests essential steps or elements that are not recited in the body of the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative and subjective terminology — acceptability depends on whether POSITA would understand the scope (MPEP 2173.05(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of relative terminology, including terms of degree or '...-like' expressions, does not automatically render a claim indefinite; acceptability depends on whether one of ordinary skill would understand what is claimed in light of the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For subjective or relative terms (e.g., 'increased yield stability', 'Sumkinda-like') look to the specification for standards or comparisons that define the term. If the specification supplies a measuring standard or shows how to compare (e.g., transformed vs. untransformed cultivar), the term may be definite. If the specification and prior art leave the term's metes and bounds unclear, issue a 112(b) rejection. (See MPEP 2173.05(b) and 2173.05(b)(IV): Subjective Terms.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemplary language in claims ('such as', 'for example') may render claim scope unclear (MPEP 2173.05(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples or preferences stated in the claims (e.g., 'R is halogen, for example, chlorine'; 'a pain reliever such as aspirin') may lead to confusion over intended scope and can render the claim indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat 'such as' or 'for example' as per se indefinite; perform fact-specific analysis. Look to the specification to determine whether the exemplification is intended to be limiting. If the specification does not establish that the example is limiting, the claim may be indefinite because it's unclear whether the example narrows the broader term or is merely illustrative. If appropriate, suggest deleting the exemplary phrase to obviate the rejection. (Slides provide multiple historical examples of problematic exemplary claim language and recommend amendment to delete such phrasing.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain meaning rule and sources of meaning (2111.01(I))
rubrics_metrics.description: Under BRI, words of a claim must be given their ordinary and customary meaning as understood by those of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention, unless the specification indicates otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To determine plain meaning, consult the claim language itself, the specification (including any special definitions), drawings, and the prior art. If the applicant acts as its own lexicographer, a clear special definition in the specification controls claim meaning; absent that, use ordinary meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble weight — determine whether preamble limits the claim (MPEP 2111.02)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide if the preamble gives 'life, meaning, and vitality' to the claim so that it should be construed as a limitation; if the body of the claim fully sets forth the limitations, the preamble may be non-limiting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze the preamble in the context of the entire claim. If the preamble merely states a purpose or intended use and the claim body includes all limitations, the preamble is not limiting; if it is necessary to make the claim definite, treat it as a limiting element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and content when writing the rejection (form paragraph guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing the rejection the examiner should explain their conclusion, include the detailed BRI analysis that provides a clear record of the systematic analysis, and, where appropriate, suggest how to overcome the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the recommended form paragraph(s) illustrated in the training: state the statutory basis (35 U.S.C. 112(b)), explain why the specific phrase lacks antecedent basis or otherwise renders the claim indefinite, cite the specification paragraphs relied upon, and, if possible, indicate an amendment that would obviate the rejection (e.g., amend 'said protein nanopores' to 'said nanopores' or delete 'such as aspirin'). If no helpful suggestion exists, do not invent one; still provide the full factual analysis and conclusion. The detailed BRI analysis should be on the record to enhance clarity of prosecution history.
